title: The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas
summary:
In Ursula K. Le Guin's 1973 story, Omelas is a city of real and uncomplicated joy, holding its Festival of Summer. But its happiness depends on one child, kept alone in a dark cellar, dirty and afraid. Everyone in Omelas knows. If the child were brought up into the sunlight and comforted, all the prosperity and beauty and delight of Omelas would wither: those are the terms. Most who go and see the child are shocked, and in time come to accept it. But some walk out of the city, alone, and do not come back. The story does not say where they go.

Le Guin said the idea came from William James, who asked whether we would accept a world of millions kept permanently happy on the one condition that a certain lost soul, far off, should suffer lonely torture. The story is often read against utilitarian reasoning. Some readers ask whether walking away does anything for the child, and whether the harder answer is to stay and try to change the terms.
citations: Ursula K. Le Guin, "The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas," in New Dimensions 3, ed. Robert Silverberg (1973); reprinted, with her note on James, in The Wind's Twelve Quarters (1975)
